subQuestions.questionText:
Select the term in Column B that best matches the description in Column A. Each letter may be used only once.

COLUMN A:
(a) Male organ that produces sperm
(b) Muscular sac that surrounds the testes
(c) State in which the penis is filled with blood under pressure and becomes rigid and enlarged
(d) A coiled tube on the outside of a testis that carries and stores sperm
(e) The part on the penis that is removed during a circumcision
(f) The tube that carries sperm from the testes to the urethra
(g) A gland that produces a fluid that has fructose to provide energy for the sperm
(h) A fluid that contains sperm cells and secretions from the male reproductive glands
(i) Expulsion of semen from the male body

COLUMN B:
A Epididymis  B Sperm duct  C Ejaculation  D Foreskin  E Testes  F Semen  G Penis  H Erection  I Seminal vesicle  J Scrotum
subQuestions.memoText:
(a) E — testes
(b) J — scrotum
(c) H — erection
(d) A — epididymis
(e) D — foreskin
(f) B — sperm duct
(g) I — seminal vesicle
(h) F — semen
(i) C — ejaculation
(1 mark each)

subQuestions.questionText:
Which of the following best describes a community?
A All the organisms in an area interacting with the environment
B An interacting group of many different species in a common area
C The specific roles of members in a population
D Populations that can interbreed with each other
subQuestions.memoText: B — a community is an interacting group of many different species (populations) living in a common area.

options.A: All the organisms in an area interacting with the environment
options.B: An interacting group of many different species in a common area
options.C: The specific roles of members in a population
options.D: Populations that can interbreed with each other

subQuestions.questionText:
Which of the following terms refers to 'two different plant species requiring different amounts of sunlight' in a forest ecosystem?
A Primary succession
B Limiting factors
C Social organisation
D Resource partitioning
subQuestions.memoText: D — resource partitioning: species use the same resource (light) in different ways, reducing competition.

subQuestions.questionText:
Figure 1.1 shows the change in size of a population over time, divided into four regions (1–4). In which region will the birth rate far exceed mortality?
A Region 1
B Region 2
C Region 3
D Region 4
(Refer to Figure 1.1 in the answer booklet.)
subQuestions.memoText: B — Region 2 (the exponential / log growth phase), where births greatly exceed deaths.

subQuestions.questionText:
Which of the options (A, B, C or D) correctly shows the carrying capacity of the population in Figure 1.1?
(Refer to Figure 1.1 and the four marked options in the answer booklet.)
subQuestions.memoText: C — the line drawn level with the plateau / stationary phase of the growth curve.

subQuestions.questionText:
A biologist sampled impala using mark-recapture. First capture: 62 impala trapped and marked with ear tags. Second capture two weeks later: 56 impala, of which 28 had ear tags. What is the estimated size of the impala population?
A 25
B 31
C 118
D 124
subQuestions.memoText: D — 124. Population = (first marked × second sample) ÷ recaptured marked = (62 × 56) ÷ 28 = 124.

subQuestions.questionText:
The Western Leopard Toad breeds by the female laying thousands of eggs in water and the male depositing sperm where the eggs were laid. Which statement is true regarding the Western Leopard Toad?
A External fertilisation and oviparous
B Internal fertilisation and oviparous
C External fertilisation and ovoviviparous
D Internal fertilisation and ovoviviparous
subQuestions.memoText: A — external fertilisation (sperm meets egg in the water) and oviparous (lays eggs; development outside the body).

subQuestions.questionText: Figure 1.4 shows members of different castes in a termite colony: A Queen, B Soldier, C Worker. Fill in the table to describe any ONE role of each caste in the termite colony.
subQuestions.memoText:
A Queen — produces eggs / reproduces.
B Soldier — defends / protects the colony; kills predators.
C Worker — collects food, feeds the queen and larvae, repairs and cleans the nest, cares for the young, cultivates food.
(1 mark each)

subQuestions.questionText: Identify and describe how any ONE structural feature of the soldier termite helps it perform its role effectively.
subQuestions.memoText: 1 mark for the structure + 1 mark for linking it to function, e.g.: soldiers have a large, hardened head to block tunnels and defend the colony; OR large, sharp mandibles / pincers to attack invaders.

subQuestions.questionText:
For each row, decide which item(s) relate to the term, using: A — only item 1; B — only item 2; C — both; D — neither.
(a) Term: Umbilical artery. 1: Contains oxygenated blood. 2: Transports blood from the amnion to the foetus.
(b) Term: Placenta. 1: Attached to the wall of the uterus. 2: Produces hormones to maintain pregnancy.
(c) Term: Embryo. 1: Has fully developed organ systems. 2: Formed after implantation of the blastocyst.
(d) Term: Amniotic fluid. 1: Protects the foetus by absorbing shock. 2: Maintains the temperature around the foetus.
(e) Term: Mammary gland. 1: Is the target organ of prolactin. 2: Secretes FSH.
subQuestions.memoText:
(a) D — the umbilical artery carries deoxygenated blood from the foetus to the placenta (not from the amnion).
(b) C — both.
(c) B — the embryo is formed after implantation; fully developed organ systems describe the foetus.
(d) C — both.
(e) A — the mammary gland is the target organ of prolactin; it does not secrete FSH.
(1 mark each)

subQuestions.questionText:
Figure 1.5 shows the levels of four hormones during pregnancy and birth. Describe and explain a reason for the changes in the hormone levels of oxytocin and prolactin between weeks 30 and 40 of pregnancy.
(Refer to Figure 1.5 in the answer booklet.)
subQuestions.memoText: Oxytocin: rises steeply (near week 40) — to stimulate / strengthen uterine (myometrial) contractions and begin labour (2). Prolactin: rises — to stimulate the mammary glands to produce milk (lactation) ready for feeding the newborn (2). (Each hormone: level described + reason explained.)

subQuestions.questionText:
Two population pyramids (country A and country B) are shown. For each statement decide whether it is A — supported, B — contradicted, or C — neither supported nor contradicted by the information:
(a) In country B, the percentage of the female population aged 20–24 is between 4% and 6%.
(b) There are more males than females between ages 80 and 84 in country A.
(c) The life expectancy of the population in country A is lower than in country B.
(d) The pyramid of country A represents a more developed country.
(e) Countries A and B have the same ecological footprint.
(f) Country A has a lower birth rate than country B.
(Refer to the population pyramids in the answer booklet.)
subQuestions.memoText:
(a) A
(b) B
(c) B
(d) A
(e) C
(f) A
(1 mark each)

subQuestions.questionText: Name and describe the sampling method that the South African government uses to collect the information needed to construct a population pyramid for South Africa.
subQuestions.memoText: Direct count / census (compulsory) (1) + one further detail (1): every household is visited and its members interviewed; information on the number of people, their ages, sexes, occupations and incomes is collected; it is carried out by government employees.

subQuestions.questionText: Suggest TWO reasons why it is important for the government to collect information about the age and sex distribution of the population.
subQuestions.memoText: Any 2 (1 mark each): to plan infrastructure (roads, housing); to decide how tax money should be spent; to understand population growth; to plan schools, medical facilities and hospitals; to plan social grants and welfare; to plan job creation / employment.

subQuestions.questionText:
Sugarcane flowers have a carpel with two feathered stigmas and three very long stamens attached to the carpel at the ovary; it is a wind-pollinated, cross-pollinating species. On the diagram of the carpel provided:
(a) Draw in the stamens to complete the sugarcane flower as described.
(b) Label the filament and anther of any one stamen you have drawn.
(c) Place the letter P on any part of the diagram where pollination would occur.
(d) Label the ovary of the flower.
subQuestions.memoText:
(a) Three stamens drawn (1), with filament and anther longer than the carpel (1), attached to the carpel anywhere on the ovary (1).
(b) Filament labelled (1); anther labelled (1).
(c) 'P' placed anywhere on a (feathered) stigma (1).
(d) Ovary labelled — must not be on the sepal (1).

subQuestions.questionText:
Complete the table of differences between asexual and sexual reproduction by choosing the correct option for each cell:
 | Asexual | Sexual
Energy use | low / high | low / high
Number of parents | one / two | one / two
Gametes produced | yes / no | yes / no
subQuestions.memoText:
Energy use: low (asexual) | high (sexual)
Number of parents: one (asexual) | two (sexual)
Gametes produced: no (asexual) | yes (sexual)
(1 mark per correct row)

subQuestions.questionText: Sugarcane is usually grown from stem cuttings (Figure 1.7) rather than from seed. Explain the advantages for a farmer of growing sugarcane from stem cuttings rather than from seed.
subQuestions.memoText: Any 4 (or 2 well explained): stem cuttings are easy and not labour-intensive; the farmer can select plants with a known, desirable phenotype, so offspring are predictable and uniform; asexual reproduction is more reliable because sexual reproduction (seed set) is very low in sugarcane; no wait for seed production, so a shorter time to harvest; more profitable — no need to buy or collect seed; faster reproduction, and multiple plants can develop from one multi-budded cutting (higher productivity).

subQuestions.questionText:
Figure 1.8 shows endocrine glands in the human body, numbered 1–6 (plus the pancreas). Select the number that best matches each statement (numbers may be used more than once):
(a) Regulates blood glucose levels
(b) Produces testosterone
(c) Produces hormones that regulate many other endocrine glands
(d) TSH targets this gland
(e) Stops producing insulin, which results in diabetes type 1
(f) Secretes thyroxin to regulate metabolism
(g) The adrenal gland
(Refer to Figure 1.8 in the answer booklet.)
subQuestions.memoText:
(a) 4 (pancreas)
(b) 6 (testis)
(c) 1 (pituitary)
(d) 2 (thyroid)
(e) 4 (pancreas)
(f) 2 (thyroid)
(g) 3 (adrenal gland)
(1 mark each; numbers as per the memo key)

subQuestions.questionText:
Figure 1.9 gives the average brain volume of some hominid species:
Australopithecus afarensis 380 cm³; Australopithecus africanus 400 cm³; Homo habilis 600 cm³; Homo erectus 1 000 cm³; Homo sapiens 1 350 cm³.
Plot a bar graph of this data on the graph paper provided, with the hominids in order of increasing brain volume.
subQuestions.memoText: Marks (8): heading e.g. "Graph showing the average brain volume of some hominid species" (1); x-axis labelled "Hominid species" (1); y-axis labelled "Average brain volume" (1) with unit cm³ (1); suitable y-axis scale (1); bar graph with equal-width bars that do not touch (1); correct plotting of all five bars, e.g. A. africanus at 400 cm³ and H. sapiens at 1 350 cm³, in order of increasing volume (2).

subQuestions.questionText: Name the hominid listed in the table (Figure 1.9) that was known to first use and control fire.
subQuestions.memoText: Homo erectus (accept Homo sapiens).

subQuestions.questionText: Explain why the ability to use and control fire is considered a significant development in hominid evolution.
subQuestions.memoText: Any 2 (or 1 well explained): a source of warmth allowed hominids to move into and inhabit colder climates; protection from predators; cooking made a wider range of foods (especially meat) edible and easier to digest, improving nutrition and brain development; better tools/weapons could be made; light extended social time at night and controlling fire required planning and co-operation.

subQuestions.questionText: Place an X on YOUR graph, between the bars, to show the most likely position of Australopithecus sediba according to brain volume.
subQuestions.memoText: X placed anywhere between Australopithecus africanus and Homo habilis (i.e. a brain volume between ~400 and ~600 cm³).

subQuestions.questionText: Bipedalism is a distinguishing feature of the hominids in Figure 1.9; Figure 1.10 shows skeletal features associated with bipedalism (skull, posture, hip, leg, feet). Select any THREE features shown and complete the table: describe the physical feature (column A) and state its importance for bipedalism (column B).
subQuestions.memoText:
Any 3, each: feature described (1) + importance for bipedalism (1). Examples:
• Foramen magnum in the centre / directly under the skull → head balanced on top of the vertebral column for an upright posture.
• S-shaped (curved) spine → supports and balances the weight of the upper body and absorbs the shock of walking.
• Femur angled inwards towards the knee → brings the feet under the body's centre of gravity, aiding balance.
• Short, arched foot bones → act as a lever/spring for energy-efficient walking and support the body's weight.
• Broad, short (bowl-shaped) pelvis → supports the abdominal organs and body weight and lowers the centre of gravity.
• Big toe aligned with the other toes (non-opposable) → allows an efficient push-off during walking.

subQuestions.questionText: Figure 2.1 is a micrograph of a single sperm cell entering an ovum, with sperm parts numbered 1, 2 and 3. Give the biological term that describes the process of a sperm cell entering an ovum.
subQuestions.memoText: Fertilisation.

subQuestions.questionText: State where in the female's reproductive system this process would most likely occur.
subQuestions.memoText: In the Fallopian tube / oviduct.

subQuestions.questionText:
Provide labels for the parts of the sperm numbered:
(a) 2
(b) 3
(Refer to Figure 2.1 in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText:
(a) 2 — middle piece / mid-piece (1).
(b) 3 — head (1).

subQuestions.questionText: What is the purpose of the many mitochondria found in the part numbered 2 (middle piece)?
subQuestions.memoText: To release energy (ATP) for the movement / whipping of the tail so the sperm can swim through the female reproductive tract.

subQuestions.questionText: Explain how the sperm enters the ovum.
subQuestions.memoText: Any 3 (3 marks): the acrosome of the sperm head contains digestive enzymes; these enzymes are released when the sperm contacts the ovum; they break down / digest the outer layers (membrane) of the ovum; the sperm nucleus then passes into the cytoplasm of the ovum.

subQuestions.questionText: Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS) is a condition in which the ovaries produce increased amounts of male sex hormones, causing many small fluid-filled cysts to form and interrupting the menstrual cycle. It affects 1 in 10 women of child-bearing age; the pill or hormonal patch is used to lower the raised LH and FSH to normal. List any TWO symptoms of a woman with PCOS.
subQuestions.memoText: Any 2 (1 mark each): missed / irregular (painful) periods; infertility; acne; increased facial or body hair; weight gain; depression; mood swings.

subQuestions.questionText:
(a) Name the gland that secretes FSH and LH.
(b) Where in the body is this gland situated?
subQuestions.memoText:
(a) The pituitary gland / hypophysis (1).
(b) In the brain — attached to / just below the hypothalamus (between the two lobes of the brain) (1).

subQuestions.questionText: Calculate the percentage of women of child-bearing age who suffer from PCOS. Show all working.
subQuestions.memoText: 1/10 × 100 = 10% (working + correct answer = 2 marks).

subQuestions.questionText:
Refer to Figures 2.2(a) and (b) — hormone concentrations and the ovarian cycle in women with PCOS and in women with regular menstrual cycles. Tabulate any THREE differences in the menstrual cycles of women with regular cycles compared with women with PCOS.
(Refer to Figure 2.2 in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Marks: heading + column headings + table format + 3 correct comparative differences (6). Examples:
Women with PCOS | Women with a regular cycle
No ovulation / follicles form cysts | Ovulation occurs / an ovum is released
LH stays high and does not fluctuate (≈15 µg/L) | LH is lower than FSH and peaks near day 14 (≈10 µg/L)
FSH stays low and does not fluctuate (<5 µg/L) | FSH is slightly higher than LH and peaks near day 14 (>10 µg/L)
Missed / irregular menstruation | Regular menstruation
Follicles develop into cysts | Follicles develop normally

subQuestions.questionText: Most oral contraceptive pills contain both progesterone and oestrogen. What effect do these hormones have on the LH levels in the PCOS menstrual cycle?
subQuestions.memoText: They lower / decrease the LH levels (by negative feedback on the pituitary).

subQuestions.questionText: By referring to FSH and LH levels, explain why women with PCOS may be infertile.
subQuestions.memoText: 3 marks: LH levels remain high with no surge / peak (1); FSH levels remain very low (1); so follicle / egg development is not stimulated and no ovum is released — no ovulation, therefore infertility (1).

subQuestions.questionText: Suggest how living with PCOS may have a social and/or cultural impact on women.
subQuestions.memoText: Any 2 (or 1 well explained): painful periods may cause absenteeism from work or school; cultural stigma around difficulty conceiving / being expected to have children and continue the family line; the financial cost of treating symptoms or of assisted reproduction (IVF); emotional strain from mood swings and depression.

subQuestions.questionText:
Carp (Cyprinus carpio) are a valuable freshwater food fish whose wild numbers have fallen due to human interference. An artificial breeding programme tested two synthetic hormones (X and Y) against a saline control for increasing ovulation in 36 mature female carp.
(a) State TWO reasons why setting up an artificial breeding programme for carp is important.
(b) Suggest a human activity that would impact the wild populations of carp.
subQuestions.memoText:
(a) Any 2 (1 mark each): carp are an important food source; wild populations are declining; to conserve the species; to produce more offspring / restock.
(b) Any one: overfishing; pollution; pesticide use; urban development; habitat fragmentation or loss; introduction of invasive species.

subQuestions.questionText: Carp are considered an r-strategy species. Provide any THREE features of a typical r-strategy species.
subQuestions.memoText: Any 3 (1 mark each): large numbers of offspring / eggs produced; short gestation / development period; reach sexual maturity quickly; short lifespan / life expectancy; few offspring reach maximum lifespan; little or no parental care; exponential population growth.

subQuestions.questionText: What is the purpose of the saline treatment being given to one group of female carp?
subQuestions.memoText: 2 marks: it is the control group; it is used to compare against the hormone treatments and to verify that any effect is due to the independent variable (the type of hormone) and not the injection itself.

subQuestions.questionText: State TWO ways in which this investigation can be improved so that the results can be published in a scientific journal.
subQuestions.memoText: Any 2 (1 mark each): increase the sample size (number of fish per treatment); repeat the investigation several times to verify the results; test more hormone types and/or a range of hormone concentrations; have the results peer-reviewed.

subQuestions.questionText: Refer to the table in Figure 2.3(b) [Hormone X: 12 fish, 5 ovulated, 1519 eggs, 927 offspring reaching maturity; Hormone Y: 12 fish, 9 ovulated, 2457 eggs, 1941 offspring reaching maturity; Saline: 12 fish, 1 ovulated, 400 eggs, 20 offspring reaching maturity]. Suggest which treatment is most suitable for increasing carp numbers. Provide data to support your answer.
subQuestions.memoText: Hormone Y (must have) (1) + any 2 supporting points, at least one quoting data (3): more fish ovulated (9 vs 5 with X, 1 with saline); more eggs produced (2457 vs 1519 with X); the highest number of offspring reached maturity (1941 vs 927 with X, 20 with saline).

subQuestions.questionText: The Galápagos finches are all dark-coloured with similar body proportions but differ in body size and beak size and shape; each species lives in a specific niche, and all evolved from one ancestral species that colonised the islands. Name the biologist who studied the Galápagos finches and proposed natural selection as a mechanism for evolution.
subQuestions.memoText: (Charles) Darwin.

subQuestions.questionText: How would a biologist determine if two finch birds belonged to the same species?
subQuestions.memoText: Any 2 (1 mark each): check whether they are genetically similar / share DNA sequences; observe morphological similarity (body shape, beak size and shape); see whether they interbreed / mate; check whether mating produces viable, fertile offspring.

subQuestions.questionText:
(a) Explain the meaning of an ecological 'niche'.
(b) Refer to Figure 3.1 and describe how occupying different niches enables each finch species to survive.
(Refer to Figure 3.1 in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText:
(a) 2 marks: the niche is the full set of resources and conditions a species needs (its role and use of the habitat) that allows it to maintain a viable population.
(b) Any 3 (3 marks): the different beak sizes and shapes let each species use food resources differently; access to resources is varied; so the species do not compete directly for the same food (e.g. one eats seeds, another eats insects); they also do not compete for the same space — competition between species is reduced.

subQuestions.questionText: Are the different finches on the islands an example of convergent or divergent evolution? Give a reason for your answer.
subQuestions.memoText: Divergent evolution (compulsory) (1) + reason (1): all the species are derived from one ancestral species / share a common ancestor and have become structurally different (different beaks) as they adapted to different niches (adaptive radiation).

subQuestions.questionText: Why are islands like the Galápagos Islands suitable places for speciation to occur?
subQuestions.memoText: Any 2 (2 marks): islands are isolated and hard to reach, with the ocean acting as a geographical barrier, so colonising species become reproductively isolated; resources may be limited, forcing diversification to avoid direct competition; there are many empty niches available, giving the opportunity for adaptive radiation.

subQuestions.questionText: Name and describe TWO lines of evidence for the theory of evolution.
subQuestions.memoText:
Any 2, each: line of evidence named (1) + described (1). Examples:
• Fossil evidence — preserved remains/traces of past organisms that can be dated to show a sequence of change over time.
• Biogeography — the distribution of related species across the world; closely related species are found in nearby regions, having descended from a common ancestor.
• Comparative anatomy — homologous structures indicate common ancestry.
• Comparative embryology — similarities in embryonic development point to shared ancestry.
• DNA / molecular biology — the more DNA or protein sequence two species share, the more closely related they are.
• Vestigial structures — reduced, non-functional versions of structures that are functional in relatives suggest common ancestry.

subQuestions.questionText: Grade 12 students used instruments (1–3) to represent bird beaks and objects (a–d) to represent food types, picking up as many food objects as possible in 5 minutes (Figure 3.2). What principle of evolution is this investigation simulating?
subQuestions.memoText: Natural selection / survival of the fittest.

subQuestions.questionText: Give the dependent variable in this investigation.
subQuestions.memoText: The number (amount) of food objects captured / picked up (accept: the type of food picked up).

subQuestions.questionText:
During the simulation, some students stole objects from other students. Choose which option represents this concept in nature. Write only the correct letter.
A predation
B competition
C adaptation
subQuestions.memoText: B — competition.

subQuestions.questionText: A student hypothesises that the peg instrument will pick up the least number of rice grains in 5 minutes. Suggest why the peg would be less effective at picking up the rice grains compared with the forceps.
subQuestions.memoText: 1 fact about the peg + 1 fact about the forceps + 1 other (3 marks): the tip of the peg is too thick / blunt / indented to grip a small rice grain (or the rice grain is too small for the peg's gap); the peg's grip point is too far back, leaving too little room; the forceps have fine, pointed tips allowing a precise grip and a wider, easier opening, so they pick up rice grains faster.

subQuestions.questionText: In your opinion, does the simulation represent the principles of natural selection correctly? Give a well-explained reason for your answer.
subQuestions.memoText: A reasoned answer (2 marks). Yes: variation in beak type is represented by the different instruments; the struggle for survival is represented by the time limit and competition for food; a poorly adapted 'beak' captures little food and would not survive. OR No: reproduction and the inheritance of variation are not represented — the instruments cannot reproduce or pass on traits.

subQuestions.questionText: Explain what is meant by Lamarck's theory of acquired characteristics.
subQuestions.memoText: 2 marks: organisms change / develop structures during their lifetime in response to using or not using them (use and disuse) to adapt to the environment; these acquired changes are then passed on to the offspring.

subQuestions.questionText: Lamarck's theory was rejected by the scientific community, yet it is still taught in the study of evolution. What value is there in learning about Lamarck?
subQuestions.memoText: Any 3 (3 marks): it shows how biological ideas have changed over time; his work gave other scientists (e.g. Darwin) ideas to build on and test; it shows what mistakes were made (acquired phenotypic changes are not inherited); it encourages open-mindedness and critical thinking; some of his observations were correct — living species differ from fossils, so species do change, and the environment does affect phenotype; it highlights that scientific ideas must be testable.

subQuestions.questionText: Leucospermum tottum and Leucospermum arenarium are two 'pincushion' protea species that grow in the same areas of the South-Western Cape but are reproductively isolated and arose by sympatric speciation. L. tottum has pink-orange flowers on upright stems, flowers late spring to early summer, and is bird-pollinated; L. arenarium has pale yellow flowers near ground level on downward stems, flowers late winter to early summer, and is mouse-pollinated. Explain the difference between allopatric and sympatric speciation.
subQuestions.memoText: 2 marks: allopatric speciation is the formation of new species when populations are separated by a physical / geographical barrier; sympatric speciation is the formation of new species while the populations continue to live in the same geographic area.

subQuestions.questionText: Describe TWO ways in which reproductive isolation is brought about in the two pincushion protea species.
subQuestions.memoText: Any 2, each fact + description (4 marks): different flowering seasons — pollen is produced at different times (L. tottum late spring–early summer; L. arenarium late winter–early summer), so cross-pollination is unlikely; different pollinators and flower positions — L. tottum has upright, bird-pollinated flowers while L. arenarium has near-ground, mouse-pollinated flowers, so pollen is not transferred between the species.

subQuestions.questionText:
Figure 3.4 is a phylogenetic tree showing the evolutionary relationships between some members of the Proteaceae family.
(a) Which species, powderpuffs or spiderheads, are more closely related to the vexators? Give a reason for your answer.
(b) Approximately how long ago did the pincushions and silkypuffs diverge?
(c) Which species is the oldest amongst all the Proteaceae?
(Refer to Figure 3.4 in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText:
(a) Powderpuffs (1) — they share a more recent common ancestor with the vexators / the divergence (speciation) point between powderpuffs and vexators is more recent (1).
(b) About 80 million years ago (2).
(c) The white trees (1).

subQuestions.questionText: In 1900 there were about 10 million wild African elephants (Loxodonta africana); by 2016 the estimate was about 415 000. Numbers were estimated using aerial surveys and transect sampling. Elephants need large ranges, and most populations are now confined to reserves linked by 'corridors'. List THREE criteria that need to be met to consider the African elephants a 'population'.
subQuestions.memoText: The individuals must: be of the same species (all Loxodonta africana) (1); live in the same / a defined area (1); be able to interbreed and produce viable offspring (1).

subQuestions.questionText:
Refer to Figure 4.1(a) — elephant populations in Africa from 1800 to the present day.
(a) Describe the trend in the graph.
(b) Which of the following (immigration, emigration, mortality or birth rate) is most likely responsible for this trend?
(c) How many elephants were living in Africa in 1920?
(Refer to Figure 4.1(a) in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText:
(a) 2 marks: the elephant population has decreased over time (from ~10 million in 1800 to ~0,4 million by 2015) — a steady decline (answer must refer to both variables and the relationship).
(b) Mortality (1).
(c) About 5 million (1) — read from the graph.

subQuestions.questionText: Discuss THREE possible reasons for the change in elephant populations in Africa since the 1800s.
subQuestions.memoText: Any 3 well-explained (2 marks each): human population expansion, urbanisation and farming converting savannah habitat, causing habitat loss and fragmentation; commercial hunting and poaching for ivory, meat and skins; wars and conflict leading to hunting of elephants; creation of reserves and fences that reduce and fragment elephant range and change migration routes; culling policies to match reserve carrying capacity; disease or parasite infestation lowering fertility and raising deaths; climate change / drought reducing food and water.

subQuestions.questionText: Suggest why conservationists would want to establish corridors between smaller nearby conservation areas.
subQuestions.memoText: Any 2 (1 mark each): improve access to food and resources; increase the range available while avoiding roads and human infrastructure; allow natural migration routes; help seed dispersal and let vegetation recover from grazing (reduce local habitat destruction and soil erosion); increase genetic variation by allowing interbreeding between the separated populations.

subQuestions.questionText: Explain TWO possible advantages of using aerial surveys to determine elephant population sizes.
subQuestions.memoText: Any 2 explained (2 marks each): large areas can be surveyed quickly, so it is less time-consuming and more efficient than surveying on foot; areas that are difficult to reach on the ground can be covered, improving reliability; it is safer — it avoids close encounters with elephants and other dangerous wildlife; elephants are large and slow, so they are easy to spot and count from the air.

subQuestions.questionText: Why is it important that the transects or quadrats are selected randomly when biologists perform the sampling method?
subQuestions.memoText: Any 2 (2 marks): to eliminate bias / give every part of the area an equal chance of being sampled; populations are not always evenly distributed, so random placement improves the validity and reliability of the estimate and allows an accurate conclusion.

subQuestions.questionText:
Fires can occur in game reserves and then new plants recolonise the burnt area.
(a) Is recolonisation by plants of an area destroyed by fire an example of primary or secondary succession? Give a reason for your answer.
(b) What is the term used to describe the first plants and animals that appear in an area after a fire?
subQuestions.memoText:
(a) Secondary succession (compulsory) (1) + reason (1): soil is still present / colonisation is not on bare rock; seeds and plant parts remain in the soil, and plants existed there before.
(b) Pioneer species / colonisers (1).

subQuestions.questionText: Figure 4.2 shows a herd of elephants (matriarch, sisters and older daughters, young calves) with a definite social structure. Describe how elephants benefit from living in a herd.
subQuestions.memoText: Any 4 (or 2 well explained): more individuals means predators are spotted sooner and the herd can surround / intimidate them (increased protection); calves are placed in the centre of the herd and defended by the adults (better care of the young); more members searching improves access to food and water; the herd meets the elephants' social needs and allows relationships to develop (elephants are highly social).

subQuestions.questionText: Name the type of competition that exists within a herd of elephants and explain your answer.
subQuestions.memoText: Intraspecific competition (1) — the elephants in the herd all belong to the same species (Loxodonta africana) and compete for the same resources (food, water, mates) (1).

subQuestions.questionText:
(a) Identify ONE density-dependent factor that will limit the growth of elephant populations.
(b) Explain how this density-dependent factor limits the growth of an elephant population.
subQuestions.memoText:
(a) Any one: lack of food; limited space / habitat; increase in disease; lack of mates; lack of drinking water; predators (1).
(b) Explanation must match (a) (1), e.g.: lack of food → elephants die of starvation; limited space → vegetation is destroyed and there is nowhere to raise young; more disease → poor health and death; lack of mates → lower reproductive rate; lack of water → death from dehydration.

subQuestions.questionText: Lions are one of the few predators that will attack an elephant, usually only when other herbivores such as springbok are scarce (Figure 4.3). Sketch a simple graph to show the relationship between lions and springbok in a game reserve over time. Label the graph lines representing the lion and the springbok, and provide a heading for the graph.
subQuestions.memoText: Marks (5): heading e.g. "Graph showing the predator–prey relationship between lions and springbok over time" (1); x-axis labelled "Time" (1); y-axis labelled "Population size / number of animals" (1); two out-of-phase oscillating curves with the prey (springbok) line above the predator (lion) line (1); the predator peaks lagging behind (following) the prey peaks (1).

subQuestions.questionText: Explain the role of lions in maintaining healthy prey populations.
subQuestions.memoText: Any 3 (3 marks): lions remove old, weak and diseased individuals, so the strongest survive to reproduce and the prey population stays genetically fit; this reduces the number of hosts available to parasites and limits overgrazing so vegetation can recover; as a keystone predator, lions keep prey numbers below carrying capacity and help maintain biodiversity.
